faq.q: Why did a notification email arrive later than the notification in my Inbox?

segments.t: To avoid sending you a separate email for every update, Attio can wait a short time before emailing a notification and combine it with others into one email. Requests that need your response are emailed right away.

faq.q: Why didn’t I get a notification for a task created via the API or another external source?

segments.t: Attio only sends task notifications for tasks created inside the app. Tasks created externally, such as through the API, intentionally don't trigger notifications. This prevents unwanted notification spam in cases where large numbers of tasks are created automatically.

Once Attio is connected to Aircall, a note will automatically be added to a person's record in Attio within a few minutes of any successful call made through Aircall, even if the call wasn't initiated from Attio. Notes are also created for inbound calls.

lines.t: For call notes to sync, the person record must already exist in Attio with the correct phone number. The integration won’t create new records, and calls made before a record was created will not be synced.

segments.t: Notes created from Aircall will include:
The name of the team member who placed the call in the title
The date and time (in UTC time zone) that the call was placed
Whether or not the call was answered
Any notes taken within Aircall during the call
You can use Aircall blocks in
to trigger automations when calls or messages end, send SMS messages, and add contacts to an agent's dialer queue.
The call ended trigger fires when an Aircall call ends. Use it to automate post-call actions like updating a deal stage after a sales call, or creating a task to follow up when a voicemail is left.
Limit the trigger to a specific Aircall number. If left empty, the trigger fires for all numbers.

: The call connected. Outputs include call identity (ID, direction), timing (started at, answered at, ended at, duration), Aircall number details, contact details, phone number and contact, the agent who handled the call, recording URL, voicemail URL, comments, and tags.

: The call did not connect. Outputs include call identity (ID, direction), timing (started at, ended at), Aircall number details, contact details, phone number and contact, the agent, missed call reason (inbound only), voicemail URL if one was left, comments, and tags.

lines.t: Recording and voicemail URLs are generated asynchronously and may not be present when the trigger fires immediately after the call ends.

segments.t: The message received trigger fires when an inbound SMS, MMS, or WhatsApp message is delivered through Aircall. Use it to create follow-up tasks, update a deal stage, or alert your team on Slack when a message arrives.

faq.q: Why did my Send email step fail with a message naming a missing template variable?

segments.t: If a template is edited in Resend after you configure the step, and the edited template needs a variable you haven't set, the step fails with a message naming the missing variable, or variables. Open the step and fill in the new variable.

faq.q: Why doesn't reconnecting my Resend API key fix a "no permission" error?

segments.t: Attio doesn't verify the API key when you connect it, so a bad key won't surface until a step or the record action actually runs. An invalid or revoked key fails with "Unauthorized. Verify you have a valid API key." A key that's valid but lacks permission for a specific action fails with "Your Resend API key does not have permission to perform this action." That error means the key itself doesn't have permission for the action you're trying to run, not that the connection is broken, so reconnecting the same key sends the same permissions and won't change the result. Check the key's permissions in Resend instead.

faq.q: Why can't I use a variable for Segment or Topic?

segments.t: must be picked from a list in the step's configuration screen, so you can't use a variable for either one.

faq.q: What happens if adding a person to a segment fails?

segments.t: Attio shows a specific error message from Resend, for example if the sending domain isn't verified or the API key doesn't have permission, and keeps the dialog open so you can fix the issue and try again.

Finds the most likely work email from a company, a name, or a LinkedIn URL.
Enter a full name, or a first and last name.
Set enough information for Hunter to identify the person. That means either a LinkedIn URL on its own, or a person's name together with a company domain or company name.
A few things affect which values get used:
A LinkedIn URL is enough by itself, and anything else you set is still sent alongside it.
If you set both a company domain and a company name, the domain is used and the name is ignored.

blocks.text: When a value doesn't come through

segments.t: Any field can arrive empty, so plan for that when you use these outputs later in your workflow. If someone enters something that doesn't fit the field's type, such as a malformed email address, a phone number Attio can’t read, or letters typed into a Number field, Attio leaves the field empty rather than passing the value along.
Two field types behave in specific ways:
: Comes through as true when the submitted value is "true", in any capitalization. Anything else comes through as false.
: An empty Number field comes through as 0, not as an empty value. If you're checking whether someone entered a number, remember that a 0 might mean they left it blank.

Activating a workflow that uses this trigger registers a webhook on the selected Webflow site. Deactivating or deleting the workflow removes that webhook. Uninstalling the Webflow app removes all webhooks Attio created and revokes Attio’s access to Webflow.

lines.t: Give each form field a unique name in Webflow. If two fields share a name, only one of their values reaches your workflow and the other is dropped.

When building Zaps, you'll need to get data from one app into another. This is called field mapping. segments.t: Attio's flexibility lets you model your CRM based on how your business runs, whether that involves deals and subscriptions, funds and LPs, client projects, or anything else. This guide walks through the building blocks and shows you how to map them onto the things your business tracks.

Before we get started, it’s important to understand the building blocks available in Attio to model how your business runs. We’ll use a spreadsheet as a reference point to explain some of these concepts.
is a container for a particular type of data, like companies, people, or deals. It's the equivalent of a table in a spreadsheet. See
for what each standard object holds, and an overview of custom objects.

is a subset of records of a given object that you’re running a process against. It lets you store data on each list entry (what we call a record in a list) that lives only in the list without editing the underlying record. See

blocks.text: Choose an attribute, a view, a list, or an object

segments.t: When you’re looking to store new data in Attio, you have four core options. Here’s some guidance on how to choose between them.

Use attributes when you want to store a new piece of data about an existing object, and that piece of data is generally relevant for every (or at least most) of that object’s records, for example, a customer's renewal date (SaaS), a fund's target size (VC), or a client's monthly retainer (agency).
Use one when you need a different cut of records that already exist in an object, and the set should keep itself up to date, such as every company in a region or every deal closing this quarter.

Use one to isolate a subset of records for a process, project, or segment, and you need data or permissions that apply only in that context, such as a customer onboarding queue (SaaS), the LPs in an active fundraise (VC), or a pitch list for new business (agency).

Use one when the thing you're tracking needs its own records, with their own attributes, relationships to other records, and a history you can report on, such as partners (SaaS), funds (VC), or client projects (agency).

When in doubt, choose the lighter structure. Start with an attribute or a view, move to a list when the process needs its own data or its own permissions, and create a custom object when the think you’re tracking needs it’s own relationships or reporting. Attributes, views, lists, and objects can all be added later, which means you don't need the perfect model before your team starts working.

blocks.text: Use an attribute for a single current value

segments.t: An attribute stores data in the place your team is already looking, on an existing record. Ask whether one current value fully describes what you want to know. As an example, a company's main point of contact is a single fact about that company, so it belongs in an attribute. On the other hand, things like support escalations or renewals aren't single current values. Each one has its own date, owner, and context, so it shouldn't be stored as an attribute.

Both Objects and Lists have attributes: object attributes apply to all records of that object, whereas list attributes only apply to entries of that list. Learn more about the difference between them in

blocks.text: Use a view to segment existing records

segments.t: A view changes how records are displayed without changing the records and without creating anything new. You can create table or Kanban views, each with its own filters, sorts, and visible attributes. A single object can carry as many saved views as your team needs. On Deals, that might be a Kanban view by stage for working the pipeline, a table sorted by close date for forecasting, and a view for each rep to see their own pipeline. Because filters can reference the current user, a single shared view can show each person only their own deals.

A view is also the lightest way to give two teams different perspectives on the same data. Sales and customer success can each save their own view of the standard Companies object without duplicating a single record, and everyone stays on the same underlying records. Learn more about

blocks.text: Use a list to run a process

segments.t: A list gives a team its own working space for records without changing the records themselves. You can add records to a list manually or populate the list with a

For example, you could use a list of people to track invitees for an event. The list attributes would hold event-specific information like RSVP status and dietary requirements, which don't need to live permanently on the person record.
The records already exist in an object and you're organizing a chosen set of them for a purpose, like recruiting, onboarding, or a fundraise.
You need attributes that only apply in that context, like the role a candidate applied for or a hiring manager's rating.
You need to control who can see the data.
List access can be set to no access for some members
, while records in object views stay visible to everyone in the workspace.
The process is temporary or the process is still taking shape.

A list shows the attributes that live on its underlying object, and you can edit them directly from the list. A list built on the standard People object, for example, can show and update each person's company.
lists and how to create them

blocks.text: Decide between a view and a list

segments.t: When deciding whether to use a view or a list to segment records, the question to ask is who decides what's in the group. The records that show in a view are determined by a set of filters. You save a filter, and records join and leave on their own as their attribute values change.
The records that show in a list are specifically chosen. A person or a
adds a record, and it stays until someone removes it.
If you can write the filter, use a view. If you can't, or the group needs its own attributes or its own permissions, use a list. These examples show the split in practice:

segments.t: Lists also have their own views, which let you choose how to display the entries on that list.

blocks.text: Create a custom object for a distinct entity

segments.t: A custom object gives a concept its own records and its own attributes. Create one when the thing you're tracking passes this test: it's a real entity with its own attributes and its own relationships to other records.
A custom object also lets you guarantee data quality, which makes them especially useful when syncing data from another application or a data warehouse.

like an invoice number, which means no two records can share the same value for that attribute, useful for deduplication.

A Referral Partner is a good example, because each partner could be either a company or a person, so they can’t simply be a list of one of those objects. It’s common to track relationships between partners and multiple other objects: deals they’ve referred, key contacts, and the company they’re associated with.
Before creating one, check whether a
already fits. Standard objects arrive with built-in attributes,

Name each side of the relationship for the role it plays. A SaaS team can connect the standard Companies object to a custom Partners object as

Once records are connected, you can

Whatever your business tracks, most data sits in the standard objects. What differs is which custom object you need:

Keep the companies you sell to, their people, and your pipeline in the standard Companies, People, and Deals objects. Keep your product accounts and the people who log into them in Users and Workspaces. Consider a custom Partners object because each partner has an owner, an agreement date, and a set of accounts it introduced. Use lists for events and recruiting.
Keep portfolio companies and deal flow in the standard Companies and Deals objects, and create a custom Funds object, because each fund has its own vintage, target size, and set of LP commitments.
Keep clients in the standard Companies object, and create a custom Projects object, because one client runs several at once, each with its own budget, dates, and team.

Keep candidates in the standard People object, and create a custom Roles object, because a role has its own brief, fee, and hiring manager, and it is the thing a candidate is matched to. Also, an Applications object could store details like the date and other application data long with links to the Role, People and Company involved via relationship attributes.

Keep donors in the standard Companies and People objects, and create a custom Grants object, because each grant carries its own amount, period, and reporting requirements rather than rolling up into a single total on the donor record.
Role-based relationships let the same person record act as a client stakeholder on one project and a specialist on another, without duplicating the record.
Creating a custom object for a single value:
A customer tier only ever holds one value per company, so a Tier object would mean opening a second record to read one word. Keep it as a select attribute on the standard Companies object.
Using a text attribute where a select attribute belongs:

A text attribute accepts anything a person types, so an Industry attribute collects "Fintech", "FinTech", and "fin-tech" as three values that filter as three separate industries. A select or multi-select attribute gives your team a fixed set of options to pick from.
Encoding a relationship in a text attribute:

Typing a partner's name into a text attribute on a company looks like a link, but you can't click through to the partner record or report on every company that partner referred. Create the object and connect the two with a relationship attribute.
Creating a list where a view would do:
If a team needs the same records filtered differently, a saved view keeps the set complete and current. A list holds a fixed set that someone has to maintain.
Recreating the same data for different teams:

If sales and customer success both work with accounts, one standard Companies object with a list and a view for each team keeps everyone on the same records, where two near-duplicate objects drift apart.

faq.q: Can Attio model a business that isn't a standard sales pipeline?

segments.t: Yes, Attio is designed to support any data model. The standard Companies, People, Deals, Users, and Workspaces objects cover most GTM data, and custom objects plus relationship attributes handle everything else, from funds and LPs to grants, projects, and physical assets. If you can name your entities and describe how they relate, you can model them.

faq.q: Can I use a list attribute in more than one list?

segments.t: No, list attributes can only be used in the list where they were created. If you find yourself needing the same attribute in multiple lists, one of these approaches usually applies:
Create the attribute at the object level instead of the list level
Object attributes are shared across all lists, so creating the attribute at the object level allows you to use it anywhere. You can

Use multiple views within one same list instead of separate lists

If it doesn’t make sense to create the attribute on the object level, consider whether you could use multiple views on a single list rather than separate lists. This works well when you’re managing different segments of records that follow a similar process or track similar data. You can

A “Role” select attribute tracks which role each person applied for.

faq.q: My spreadsheet uses tags. What should they become?

segments.t: Turn each tag into an option on a select or multi-select attribute. Your team then picks from a dropdown instead of typing values, which gives you consistent spelling, colors for scanning, and clean filtering.

faq.q: Should I track my pipeline in the Deals object or a list?

segments.t: A list is a simple alternative for tracking deal flow, but the standard Deals object is the more scalable setup. Deals act as a central hub for the notes, tasks, and attributes tied to each deal, while sales lists use company records, which can become cluttered when multiple teams work with the same companies.

faq.q: Do I need to get the data model right from day one?

segments.t: No. Attributes, views, lists, and objects can all be added later, and it's normal to start with a list and move to a custom object once relationships or reporting call for it.

A data model might sound complicated, but it's really just a way to visualize, organize, and show connections between data. When you make a spreadsheet or jot down a categorized to-do list, you’re modeling your data.
Attio models your data. It allows you to organize, structure, and connect it in whichever way that suits your business, and then use your data to build business workflows and processes.
Attio’s data model has four main components:
. Getting familiar with these concepts and how they appear in your workspace is key to fully benefiting from Attio.

segments.t: Lists give you the power to organize records in whatever way works best for you. By adding records to a list, you can include additional data for each one. This data can be tailored to a specific workflow or business process, like customer onboarding or managing sales pipelines, without altering the original records themselves.

This flexibility is what makes lists so powerful. You can work with the same records in multiple contexts, customizing them for the needs of different projects or teams. All the while, the underlying records remain untouched, serving as a consistent single source of truth that keeps everyone aligned.

The same record can appear more than once in a single list. For example, if the same person applies for two different roles, they can have two separate entries in a Recruiting list, one entry per application. Both entries point to the same underlying person record, but each entry can have different values for list attributes like

segments.t: Attio is the CRM for modern go-to-market teams. It has a highly flexible data model and is easy to build with, allowing you to tailor your CRM exactly to your business model. Whether you run a high-growth PLG startup, a B2B marketplace, or sell products to distributors globally, Attio will work for you.

title: Introduction to workflows
description: Automate nearly any process inside Attio.
desc: Automate nearly any process inside Attio.

segments.t: is a set of automated rules that runs inside Attio: when something happens, take these actions. Instead of manually updating records, sending notifications, or moving data between tools, you define the logic once and Attio handles it every time the conditions are met.
You can build workflows manually using the canvas, or describe your goal in plain language and Ask Attio construct it for you.
Each run consumes workspace credits, and how many depends on the complexity of the workflow. Learn more about
Every workflow is made up of a trigger and one or more steps.
is the event that starts a workflow. Triggers include events like a record being created or updated, an attribute changing value, a recurring schedule, or a webhook from an external tool.

define what the workflow does once it's triggered. Each block performs one operation: updating a record, creating a task, sending a Slack message, enrolling someone in a sequence, making an HTTP request, and so on.

You chain blocks together on the canvas to build the full logic you need. Some blocks apply conditional logic, such as a filter that stops the run if certain conditions aren't met, or an if block that routes the run down different paths.

Workflows handle a wide range of automation use cases. For example, you could automatically notify your sales team in Slack whenever a deal is marked as won, or assign new leads to team members on a round-robin basis, or enroll a contact in an email sequence the moment they hit a specific stage in your pipeline.

Email sync, People and Company records
When you sync your email and calendar, Attio will automatically create
records for every person and company you’ve ever interacted with. It will then enrich those records with data from dozens of public sources.

Your person and company records will be automatically linked, meaning you’ll have a complete, centralized view of all your contacts at each company and how you’ve interacted with them. You’ll have access to your team’s communication history with every company and individual across time.

Attio’s communication intelligence gives you quick insights into common questions that drive day-to-day decisions. You can see how strong your relationship is with each company or person, who has the strongest relationship, and how recently you’ve been in touch. You can also see any other email and calendar interactions that have taken place.

segments.t: AI attributes can’t currently run automatically on their own. If you want AI-generated values to appear automatically as records are created or updated, you can use workflow automations with AI blocks instead.

segments.t: Use Ask Attio to create, update, and delete notes, and search notes by date, author, linked record, or content. If you do not confirm the changes, nothing is created, updated, or deleted.

or modify existing workflows from a natural language description. Describe what you want the workflow to do, including the trigger, the object or list involved, and the action, and Ask Attio constructs it on the canvas in real time. You can then review, refine, and publish the workflow.

Use Ask Attio to ask questions in multiple languages across your workspace data. You can ask questions in one language and get relevant results even if the source content, such as notes, call transcripts, or emails, is in a different language.
For example, you can ask about pricing in German and receive results related to pricing even if the original content was not written or spoken in German.

segments.t: Use Ask Attio to change your workspace's data model in natural language. Ask Attio can:
Enable the Deals, Users, and Workspaces standard objects.
Create attributes on objects, such as currency, date, status, select, and relationship attributes.

You can ask for one change or several related changes in the same message. Before it suggests anything, Ask Attio checks the objects and attributes that already exist in your workspace and follows built-in data modeling guidance. For example, it suggests enabling the Deals standard object rather than creating a custom object for deals, and it points out a similar attribute that already exists instead of creating a duplicate.

Ask Attio shows the proposed changes for your approval before it makes them. When you approve several related changes, Ask Attio applies them together: either every change is made or none are. If you reject the changes, nothing is created.

blocks.text: Add context about your data model

segments.t: While Ask Attio can access your data, it may not understand what specific objects, attributes, or workflows represent. If your prompt depends on an understanding of your data model or a specific use case, include that context directly in the prompt.
For more reliable results, structure your prompts using three sections: Context, Task, and Constraints. Before running a prompt, make sure you have answered each of the following.
Specify which objects or sources Ask Attio should use, such as companies, deals, emails, notes, call recordings, or web research.
Define any limits to the scope of the request, like “last quarter” or “active deals only”.
Describe what you want Ask Attio to do in plain language.
Focus on the outcome, such as summarizing an account, drafting a follow-up email, or identifying blockers and next steps.
Define the output format, such as bullet points, headings, or a checklist.
Set any expectations for length or tone.
Add guardrails or exclusions, like excluding inactive deals.
This structure makes prompts easier to reuse, more predictable in their results, and more consistently actionable.
You are summarizing a specific call recording. You have access to the call transcript, notes linked to the meeting, meeting participants, and other linked records.
Create a call recap that captures:
Call overview: what was the call about (1-2 sentences), primary goals of the call, outcome
Participants: who attended and their roles
Key topics: the main themes covered, grouped into 3-5 bullet sections
Next steps: the concrete next actions
Be concise and actionable, avoid long paragraphs
Keep the recap actionable, focus on what matters for follow-up
If there is no relevant call recording or meeting in context, ask the user to confirm what the relevant call or meeting is before proceeding

. This Policy is not intended to be contractual. Please refer to our

We're committed to using AI responsibly. That means following ethical guidelines built around fairness, accountability, transparency, human oversight, inclusion, and non-discrimination. We regularly review and improve how we use AI to make sure it meets best practices and industry standards.
We're open with customers about how and when we use AI. That's why we publish this Policy on our website and list AI providers that process personal data in our

We put appropriate safeguards in place to protect customer data from unauthorized access or disclosure when using AI.
Where customer data includes personal data, we process it in line with our

. We use physical and electronic safeguards to prevent personal data from being accidentally lost, misused, accessed without authorization, altered, or disclosed. We also have procedures in place to promptly notify customers in writing if we become aware of a personal data breach. Before allowing any supplier, including third-party AI providers, to access customer data, we carry out appropriate due diligence and will update our sub-processor list in line with our
We will ensure that all employees and contractors receive training on AI use and this Policy at least once a year. We will keep records to show that training has been completed.

We only build and use AI systems that are robust, secure, and safe. To deliver our services, we may use third-party AI models from providers such as Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. description: Learn how to connect AI assistants to your Attio workspace.
desc: Learn how to connect AI assistants to your Attio workspace.
toc: What you can do with Attio MCP
When to use Attio MCP or Ask Attio

segments.t: Using the Model Context Protocol, Attio MCP enables compatible AI assistants to securely access and take action on your CRM data once it has been configured and authenticated. This makes it possible to search, create, and update records, work with notes, and manage tasks in Attio using natural language.
If you are building AI powered workflows or connecting AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, or other MCP compatible clients to Attio, this is the supported way to do it.
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open standard that allows AI assistants to securely interact with external tools and data sources.
Attio’s MCP implementation provides a structured and permissioned way for AI assistants to access your workspace. Actions are authenticated and respect your existing workspace permissions.
Attio MCP is for anyone who wants to connect an external AI assistant to their Attio workspace.
This can include developers building custom workflows, as well as operators or team members who want to use AI assistants like ChatGPT or other MCP compatible clients to query or update CRM data.
If you are only using AI features inside Attio, you do not need MCP. MCP is only required when connecting an external AI assistant to your workspace.

blocks.text: What you can do with Attio MCP

segments.t: With Attio MCP, compatible AI assistants can:
Search for people, companies, deals, and other records
Create custom objects, enable standard objects, and create attributes on objects
Create, update, and delete views on objects and lists, including their filters, sorts, shown attributes, and kanban settings
Create and update lists, and update list entries
Access is scoped to your authenticated Attio account, so AI assistants can only access data and take actions that you already have permission to access in your workspace.
Attio MCP: prompts and best practices
for a range of example use cases.

blocks.text: When to use Attio MCP or Ask Attio

segments.t: Ask Attio allows you to use AI directly inside Attio. It is designed for fast, in product answers and assistance with your workspace, with no additional setup required.
Attio MCP is a good fit when you want to connect Attio to external AI assistants and workflows. For example:
Using AI assistants like ChatGPT or Claude to generate structured outputs such as sales summaries or reports based on your CRM data
Connecting Attio with other MCP enabled tools to move or sync information between systems
Using more advanced AI agent environments that can combine Attio with custom scripts or multi step automations
Ask Attio and MCP are complementary, and the best option depends on whether you are working inside Attio or connecting Attio to external systems.

segments.t: Suggestions are available on Enterprise and Ultra plans and are rolling out to workspaces gradually in November 2026. Only admins can see Attio Labs.

faq.q: What happens if I disable suggestions for the workspace?

segments.t: Attio stops reviewing workspace data and creating new suggestions. Members’ existing suggestions aren't deleted immediately, but they're withdrawn over time if they’re not actioned or dismissed.

faq.q: Are suggestions secure?

segments.t: Attio provides instructions and context to help prevent misuse, but AI can make mistakes. You should review suggestions before accepting them.

segments.t: This is your comprehensive guide to understanding and leveraging the building blocks that power workflows. Workflows gives your team complete control and flexibility to build out virtually any go-to-market process you need, right inside Attio.

We’ll break down the various triggers and actions that you can use to automate your processes. At the heart of workflows are two primary components: trigger blocks that initiate the workflow, and action blocks that execute specific tasks. For a step by step walkthrough to set up workflows, see
to understand the feature terms used in these block descriptions.

Trigger blocks are the starting point of any workflow. They determine when a specific workflow should be initiated and what data will be passed to subsequent blocks. Here is an overview of the available trigger blocks.
For a video walkthrough of the trigger blocks available in workflows, see
Use record triggers for workflows that are initiated from a specific

Executes a specified mathematical formula. Provides the formula’s result as a variable input for subsequent blocks. Supports +, -, /, and *.
Formula: Type the mathematical formula, using variables to provide the values from Number or Currency type attributes that you want to use in your calculation.
As an example, you could use a variable to input a "Quantity purchased” attribute, times a “Price” attribute, to result in the total price of all items.

One example of a use case for this block is randomly assigning things to team members. For example, if you had two Sales team members and want to route half of new leads to each member, you could generate a random number between 0 and 1, follow it by an If / else block, and when the number is over 0.5 assign to one team member, and when it’s under 0.5 assign to the other team member. If one team member should have more leads assigned than the other, you can adjust the If / else block’s condition numbers accordingly.

As a best practice, set the workspace access setting to the lowest level of access anyone in the workspace should have. Then use team and member access settings to grant additional access to the people who need it.

A member's access is based on the most permissive setting that applies to them across the workspace access setting, any teams they're part of, and any member access settings. More specific settings can only grant additional access, but they cannot reduce access below the workspace default. This means that No access settings for individual members or teams have no effect if workspace access grants a more permissive level.

For example, if workspace access is set to Full access and a member is assigned No access, they will still have Full access. If workspace access is set to Read only and one of a member's teams is assigned Read and write access, they will have Read and write access.

segments.t: Troubleshooting plays a vital role in building and managing your workflows within Attio, whether you're aiming to understand why your legacy workflow didn't run as anticipated or you simply want to track your credit usage.
To view all runs for a live or paused legacy workflow, follow these steps:
Navigate to the legacy workflow you want to troubleshoot.
Browse the list of runs and click to view details about that specific run.

The run viewer is divided into two main sections: a read-only view of the workflow on the left and a sidebar on the right that provides high-level statistics about the workflow and a list of all its runs.

By default, you will be presented with the latest run of the workflow. In the sidebar, you can see the status of each run, and hovering over each run will reveal more details such as the start and end times, as well as the number of credits consumed by the run.
Clicking on a run opens it on the canvas and allows you to review the executed blocks. In the case that the run failed, you can also access details about what went wrong.

blocks.label: View workflow runs & an example run.
blocks.alt: View workflow runs & an example run.

segments.t: Once a specific run is selected, the view of your workflow displays the list of blocks that were actually executed. For example if your workflow has an If / else block, you’ll see which path was taken and the next steps that fired.

Clicking on any block will replace the sidebar with a deeper view of the configuration. You’ll see the inputs that were set at the time of execution, as well as outputs for each block. For instance, a Formula block will display the calculated value, and a Create Record block will show the created record as well as who and when it was created.

blocks.label: Example workflows run with sidebar if/else block.
blocks.alt: Example workflows run with sidebar if/else block.

segments.t: Any block that fails to execute will be highlighted red, and clicking the failed block will show a more detailed error message to help resolve the issue and fix your workflow. Failed block executions do not count towards credit usage.
If your workflow contains a Loop block, click the < and > buttons above the block on the canvas to navigate between loop iterations.

If your workflow contains a Research record block, you can see what steps the agent took to research each question and what the outputs were. If the agent was not able to find an answer to a question, the output for that question will be empty.
Runs that are still executing can be canceled by clicking the red

button in the top right of the toolbar. This will prevent any more blocks in the run from being executed. Depending on the block, the currently executing step may still complete, and if it does it will count towards credits usage. Steps after the currently executing step will not count towards credit usage.

lines.t: Available on pro, enterprise and ultra plans.

segments.t: Sequences in Attio are automated, multi-step email campaigns. You can control timing, exit criteria, thread settings, and sender details, then draft steps using templates or AI. Once published, sequences can be launched from lists or records, with support for delegated sending.
Attio’s email sequences are well suited for sending emails to existing customers or warm leads in cases where:
Recipients expect to receive the emails.
The messages are not transactional, meaning they're not emails sent automatically in response to an action or event (such as password resets or purchase confirmations).
It is appropriate to include an unsubscribe link, which is required for all sequence emails.
Keep in mind that Attio is not an email service provider (ESP). Attio sends all emails through your synced Gmail or Microsoft account.
Here are some examples of good use cases for Attio sequences:
Nurturing inbound leads, where recipients are expecting the communication, and any individual sales rep is sending a low volume of emails
Goal-oriented workflows, such as follow-up demo calls or inviting a customer to book time with their Customer Success Manager
Here are some examples of use cases where Attio sequences should not be used:
Cold or high volume sales outreach
Business transactional emails, such as payment confirmations, password resets, security alerts, etc.

title: Email deliverability guide
description: Understand email deliverability and its impact on sending emails.
desc: Understand email deliverability and its impact on sending emails.

segments.t: Email deliverability refers to the ability of an email to successfully reach a recipient’s inbox, instead of being filtered into spam or rejected. The better deliverability a sender has, the more chance that their emails will stay out of the recipient’s spam folders.
Email delivery and email deliverability are often mistakenly used interchangeably, but they are two distinct concepts:
is the number of emails delivered to the recipient server, regardless of where emails go after that.
focuses on what happens after delivery, measuring the ability to deliver an email to its intended placement in the recipient’s inbox.

Think of a package delivery service: a package addressed to your home could be marked as delivered, even if the package was left at your neighbor’s front door. Package deliverability would be poor in this case, as the package did not reach its intended address.
As a business, understanding and monitoring your email deliverability is crucial as it directly influences the following:
: If your emails aren’t delivered to your customers' inboxes, you’re missing your opportunity to engage with your customers.

: Your email domain can earn a poor reputation based on your deliverability rates, which can harm communication across your business. If you send too many emails that bounce or end up in spam, your domain will be flagged as an untrustworthy sender by email providers.
When your team spends time reaching out to your customers via email, low deliverability means wasted effort and cost. Your audience can’t engage with your business if they don’t receive your emails.
There are several factors that determine email deliverability, working together to influence whether your email successfully reaches its intended place in the inbox:

Sender reputation is one of the most critical factors for email deliverability. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) track and score email senders based on their sending habits. If a large number of your sent email bounces, or if too many recipients mark your emails as spam, your sender reputation will be negatively impacted. A poor sender reputation means that emails you send from your domain or IP address carry a high risk of landing in the spam folder or being rejected.
There are a few best practices for maintaining a positive sender reputation:
Warm up your sending domain gradually. A consistent and gradual increase in volume signals trustworthiness, whereas erratic sending patterns can be flagged by ISPs.
Regularly monitor your IP addresses to ensure they don’t appear on any blocklists.
Analyze and address email bounces promptly. High bounce rates can indicate that you’re sending emails to invalid or outdated addresses, which ISPs typically interpret negatively.
Learn more about understanding email bounces
from providers such as Yahoo and Gmail to get insights on which users mark your emails as spam. Use this data to adjust your email campaigns and reduce spam complaints.
We recommend the following tools to help you monitor your sender reputation:

Email authentication is a framework of protocols that are used to prevent spoofing. The protocols allow you to authenticate your emails so that ISPs can trust that emails sent from your domain are really coming from your company, and not someone pretending to be you. There are three common authentication protocols, and if any of these checks fail, your emails could be marked as spam or rejected by the recipient server:
: SPF allows domain owners to specify which IP addresses are authorized to send emails on their behalf.
: DKIM adds a digital signature to your emails that helps ISPs verify that the email wasn’t tampered with during transit.

: DMARC uses SPF and DKIM (both required for this protocol) by giving domain owners the ability to instruct ISPs what to do if authentication fails. A properly configured DMARC policy improves trustworthiness and protects against spoofing.

Attio is not an email service provider, but rather sends through your email service provider, which is either Google or Microsoft. Since Attio does not interact with recipient mail servers when sending your email, you do not need to authenticate Attio as an approved sender for your domain.

We do recommend authenticating through Gmail or Microsoft (whichever email provider you’ve synced), as their servers are ultimately responsible for sending and delivering email to your audience. We recommend ensuring SPF and DKIM, at a minimum, are enabled for your domain through your provider directly.

lines.t: If you’d like to create a DMARC record for your domain, we recommend working with your domain or IT admin to do so. DMARC can harm deliverability if it’s set up incorrectly.
Note on Google and Yahoo sender requirements:
both require bulk senders to authenticate their domains using SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.
defines a bulk sender as a domain that sends emails to 5,000 or more personal Gmail addresses in a 24-hour period.

segments.t: We recommend the following tools to help you check for the presence and validity of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records on your domain:

Even with a strong sender reputation and proper email authentication in place, the content within your email can also significantly impact its deliverability. There are many pieces that factor into creating good email content that will stay out of spam. Here are some best practice guidelines:

Send content that is personalized and relevant to your audience. Use subject lines that are compelling to increase your open rate, and share content that is valuable to your audience to increase read time. Both of these factors work together to improve your sender credibility and audience engagement, and signal to ISPs that your email is not spam. Avoid re-using unsuccessful content.
Avoid spammy keywords and phrases. Using all caps, excessive punctuation (e.g., “!!!”), and
like "free," "winner," “act now,” or "guarantee," can trigger spam filters. Overuse of such terms can lead to emails being flagged as promotional or malicious.

Use links sparingly. Including too many links, suspicious-looking URLs, or using links that follow redirects will raise spam flags. Links should match the sending domain wherever possible and should be used thoughtfully.
Avoid sending attachments, especially large ones. Sending large files or an excessive amount of attachments can make your email look spammy.
Maintain a healthy text-to-image ratio. Emails that contain a lot of images and little text are often associated with spam.
Ensure you use clean, simple code. Poorly coded HTML (e.g., broken tags or excessive use of formatting) can raise flags for spam filters.
Include a clear unsubscribe link in the footer of your email, making it simple for any recipient to unsubscribe from your communications.
in all emails sent from Attio sequences.
We recommend the following tools to test how spam filters may view the content of your emails:

ISPs also track how recipients interact with your emails, making list quality another important factor for email deliverability. Keeping your contact lists clean and updated is one of the easiest ways to improve deliverability and engagement. When recipients consistently open and click on your emails, it indicates that your content is relevant and wanted, which in turn boosts your sender reputation.
Sending to outdated or unengaged recipients can hurt your sender reputation and lower engagement metrics. Here are a few best practices:
Verify that the email addresses you email are valid.
Avoid buying lists of email addresses, and regularly clean your list by removing inactive or bounced email addresses.
Avoid sending to consistently unengaged recipients.
Don’t resend emails to permanently bounced addresses.
Monitor your spam complaint and unsubscribe rate. High scores in these two areas signal to ISPs that your content is not relevant to your audience, which will lead to lower deliverability over time.
Use opt-in practices to ensure your audience is expecting to hear from you. Sending emails to people who didn’t explicitly sign up for your emails can lead to high spam complaints and low engagement.

title: Understanding email bounces
description: Analyze and resolve bounced emails for increased deliverability.
desc: Analyze and resolve bounced emails for increased deliverability.
toc: What happens when an email sent from an Attio sequence bounces?

segments.t: Email bounces are a common issue with email campaigns. Knowing how to address and prevent them is important for maintaining the health of your email campaigns and sender reputation.

An email bounces happens when an email service provider (ESP) attempts to deliver an email to the recipient’s email server, but the delivery fails or is rejected. This results in an automated bounce message, which indicates the error, being sent back to the sender. There are two types of email bounces:

: These are temporary issues, meaning your email could still be delivered after a retry. Soft bounces are commonly due to the recipient's inbox being full or a temporary problem with the recipient’s server.

: These are permanent failures, meaning the email will not be delivered no matter how many retries are attempted. Hard bounces are typically due to content, strict policy enforcement, or because the email address is invalid, non-existent, or blocked.

Most ESPs or email systems will generate a bounce report when an email is undeliverable. These reports contain important details like the recipient's email address, the time the bounce occurred, and an error code that explains why the bounce happened.
A typical bounce report might look like this:

blocks.text:
Recipient: name@example.com
Status: 5.1.1 (Bad destination mailbox address)
Diagnostic-Code: smtp; 550 5.1.1 User unknown

segments.t: This report tells us that email delivery failed permanently because the email address of the recipient (name@example.com) does not exist.
Resolving bounced emails depends on the type of bounce and the specific error code associated with it.
: Since these are temporary issues, you often don’t need to take immediate action. Monitor the bounce reports to see if the message eventually gets through.
: Your email provider will typically retry sending the email, but if it continues to bounce you may want to wait a few hours or days and try again manually.
: If the bounce persists, try reaching out to the recipient through another channel (like phone or social media) to let them know their inbox is full or their server is having issues.
: For issues like a 5.1.1 error (non-existent email), verify that the recipient's email is accurate. If possible, reach out to the person to obtain their correct address.
: If an email address is outdated or inactive, remove it from your mailing list to prevent further bounces.
is essential to maintaining a positive sender reputation.
: For 5.7.1 errors (policy rejections), check whether your emails are being flagged as spam.
Make sure your content follows best practices
, such as avoiding spammy subject lines or attaching large files.
: Some bounces happen because the recipient’s server doesn’t trust the sender's email domain.
like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC can improve deliverability.

: If you're seeing recurring bounces from multiple addresses on a single domain, it could be that the recipient’s server is blocking emails from your domain. Contact your email service provider (Google or Microsoft) or the recipient's IT department to resolve the issue.

segments.t: Links in workflow messages can point to a different page on each run, such as the deal a notification is about. To do this, add a variable to the link's URL. A variable is a placeholder for data from the trigger or an earlier block, such as a deal's name or owner, and Attio fills in its value each time the workflow runs. Much of this data comes from attributes, which store each piece of information about a record.

A system attribute that holds the web address of a record's page in Attio. Use it to link to the record the workflow is about.
Attributes that store web addresses, such as a Quote URL attribute on deals. Use them to link to pages outside Attio.

As a best practice, set the workspace access setting to the lowest level of access anyone in the workspace should have. Then use team and member access settings to grant additional access to the people who need it.

A member's access is based on the most permissive setting that applies to them across the workspace access setting, any teams they're part of, and any member access settings. More specific settings can only grant additional access, but they cannot reduce access below the workspace default. This means that No access settings for individual members or teams have no effect if workspace access grants a more permissive level.

For example, if workspace access is set to Full access and a member is assigned No access, they will still have Full access. If workspace access is set to Read only and one of a member's teams is assigned Read and write access, they will have Read and write access.

The fastest way is to let Ask Attio migrate a workflow for you, double-checking before publishing. If you'd rather rebuild yourself, the manual path is covered further down.
The new features and refined pricing we’ve introduced for new workflows make them more capable and cheaper to run, so we recommend moving your legacy workflows over.
That said, your existing legacy workflows will continue running for now. You’ll receive notice well in advance before we sunset legacy workflows.

segments.t: To test a migrated workflow, you have to publish it. You’ll need to decide what to do with the legacy workflow while you test, because it will be listening for the same trigger as the new workflow.
: while both workflows are enabled, any event that meets the trigger will kick off both workflows, which risks duplicate actions. The upside is that no actions get missed during testing.

: this prevents the two workflows duplicating the same actions, but the migrated workflow becomes the only one handling the trigger before you've confirmed it works. If it fails partway through a real event during the test, you won’t have the legacy workflow to fall back on.

For example, if your legacy workflow notifies the sales team via a Slack notification when a deal closes, and you disable the legacy workflow to test the new one, a deal that closes during the test won't notify the team if the migrated workflow doesn’t complete as expected.

Leaving the legacy workflow enabled at the same time as publishing the new one for testing is usually the lower-risk option, because duplicated actions are often less of a problem than missed actions (having two Slack messages about the same closed deal is better than no messages about the closed deal). For a high-volume trigger, or one where duplicate actions would be costly or hard to reverse, disable the legacy workflow first and test during a low-traffic window.

If your migrated workflow uses a Manual run or Record action trigger, the trade-off is smaller. Once published, the workflow runs only when you trigger it, so you can leave the legacy workflow enabled as well as enabling the migrated workflow, then run the migrated workflow with little risk of duplication.

faq.q: Can Ask Attio migrate any workflow?

segments.t: Ask Attio can migrate most workflows, and tells you about anything it couldn't translate directly so you can fix it. More complex workflows may need some manual adjustment afterward.

faq.q: Does the migrated workflow go live automatically?

segments.t: No. Ask Attio creates the new workflow but leaves it disabled. We suggest thoroughly checking the migrated workflow and checking anything that Ask Attio flagged during the build. Once you’re happy, test the newly migrated workflow first (
), then disable the legacy workflow and enable the new one (

faq.q: Do I have to migrate my legacy workflows?

segments.t: No. Legacy workflows keep running until you disable them. There's no sunset date yet, and when that changes, you'll get plenty of advance notice. That said, you can't create new legacy workflows, and new capabilities and pricing are only available in the new builder.

faq.q: Can I still edit my legacy workflows?

segments.t: Yes. Existing legacy workflows remain fully editable.

faq.q: I can't find a block I used in my legacy workflow. Where did it go?

segments.t: Some blocks have been renamed, and others absorbed into different blocks. Check the
. If/else is now called If. Prompt completion functionality is now part of the Custom Agent block.

faq.q: My legacy workflow used interaction attributes as trigger conditions. Will that work in the new builder?

segments.t: Interaction attributes can still be used as trigger conditions, but new_value and previous_value are not available as variable options for interaction-type attributes like Next interaction in the new builder.

faq.q: Can I run both workflows at the same time while testing?

segments.t: Yes, this is possible, but not recommended in every situation. In
, we cover the options you have for testing your newly migrated workflow.

faq.q: My new workflow doesn't behave the same way as the legacy version. What should I check first?

segments.t: Start with the run log in the

Verify that trigger event names use the new labels (Attribute value changed, not Attribute changed; If, not If/else), and check that variable references between blocks are correctly wired. See
for a full guide to reading run logs.

title: Overview of workflows
description: Understand what workflows are and how they're structured.
desc: Understand what workflows are and how they're structured.

segments.t: is a set of automated rules that runs inside Attio: when something happens, take these actions. Instead of manually updating records, sending notifications, or moving data between tools, you define the logic once and Attio handles it every time the conditions are met.
You can build workflows manually using the canvas, or describe your goal in plain language and let Ask Attio construct it for you.
Each run consumes workspace credits, and how many depends on the complexity of the workflow. Learn more about
Every workflow is made up of a trigger and one or more steps.
is the event that starts a workflow. Triggers include events like a record being created or updated, an attribute changing value, a recurring schedule, or a webhook from an external tool.

define what the workflow does once it's triggered. Each block performs one operation: updating a record, creating a task, sending a Slack message, enrolling someone in a sequence, making an HTTP request, and so on.

You chain blocks together on the canvas to build the full logic you need. Some blocks apply conditional logic, such as a filter that stops the run if certain conditions aren't met, or an if block that routes the run down different paths.

Workflows handle a wide range of automation use cases. For example, you could automatically notify your sales team in Slack whenever a deal is marked as won, or assign new leads to team members on a round-robin basis, or enroll a contact in an email sequence the moment they hit a specific stage in your pipeline.

The run viewer shows each run step by step so you can inspect block behavior, review run data, and diagnose failures. You can also rerun failed executions, compare retry attempts, and troubleshoot common configuration issues.
The run viewer shows a complete history of your workflow runs.

segments.t: The run viewer has two sections: a read-only workflow canvas on the left and a sidebar on the right.

The sidebar shows summary details for the selected workflow and a list of all runs. By default, the most recent run is selected. Hover over a run to reveal the runtime, start and end times, and the number of credits consumed.

Click a run to open the workflow canvas for that execution and show the blocks as they appeared when the run happened. Green arrows indicate the path that executed. Green checkmarks indicate blocks that executed successfully, and failed blocks are marked in red.
Click any block in a completed run to see a detailed view of that block’s execution in the sidebar. Scroll down to find

For example, a Formula block displays its calculated value, and a Create record block shows the created record along with who created it and when. Not all blocks display outputs.

This is often the fastest way to diagnose a workflow. In many cases, the error starts in an earlier block, even though it only becomes visible later in the run.
Any block that failed is highlighted in red on the canvas. Click a failed block to display a detailed error message in the sidebar. Failed blocks do not count toward credit usage.

segments.t: These are some of the most frequent workflow issues and how to resolve them.

A common issue occurs when a workflow updates a record in a way that triggers the same workflow again, or when two workflows repeatedly trigger each other. For example, a workflow triggered by Record updated that also updates the same record could trigger itself repeatedly.
There are a couple of ways to prevent this:
Add a Filter block immediately after the trigger with a condition
Updated by > Type > is not > Workflow
. This ensures the workflow ignores updates made by any workflow automation. This filter applies to updates from all workflows, not a specific workflow.
Scope the trigger to a specific attribute.

For Record updated, List entry updated, and Attribute value changed triggers, configure the trigger to run only when a specific attribute changes that your workflow's actions do not modify. For example, if the workflow updates Deal owner, scope the trigger to run only when Deal stage changes.

blocks.text: An attribute update isn't triggering a workflow

segments.t: If a workflow uses a Record updated or List entry updated trigger but does not fire when you expect it to, the attribute value may have been set during creation rather than updated afterward. These triggers fire only when changes happen after the record or list entry is created. If the attribute value is set at creation time, such as a deal created with the stage already set to “Won,” the trigger does not fire because the value was never updated.

To catch attribute values set at creation time, use the Attribute value changed trigger instead. This trigger fires whenever the specified attribute's state changes, including values set when the record or list entry is first created.

blocks.text: Filter conditions are returning unexpected results

segments.t: If filter conditions are not working as you expect, check the operators between your conditions. Conditions joined by
require every condition to be true, while conditions joined by
require only one to be true. When conditions are organized into groups, verify the operator both within each group and between groups. Learn more about
setting filter conditions and using condition operators
For example, a filter that checks “Deal stage is Won”
“Deal owner is Alex” will match records that meet either condition, while
matches only records that meet both.

blocks.text: A block is only processing one record or list entry

segments.t: If a block is connected directly to the output of a Find records or Find list entries block that returns multiple records or entries, the block processes only the first result by default. This is usually indicated by a warning icon on the block.
To process every matching record or list entry:
Add a Loop block after the Find records or Find list entries block.
Configure the Loop block to iterate through the returned records or list entries.
Place the block you want to run for each result inside the Loop block.
This ensures the workflow takes action on each returned record or list entry instead of only the first one. Learn
When a block fails, the error message in the run viewer indicates what went wrong. Here are common errors and how to resolve them.

blocks.text: “The provided sender has not enabled delegated sending”

segments.t: This error occurs when delegated sending is not enabled for the sender used in your workflow’s sequence. To fix it:

If you want to send emails from someone else’s address, search for and invite them as a delegated sender. They’ll receive a notification to approve the invite before emails can be sent from their address.
Once delegated sending is enabled for the sender used in your workflow, the error should no longer appear.

blocks.text: “Company records cannot be enrolled into a sequence” or similar

segments.t: Sequences send to people, not companies. Only person records can be enrolled in sequences as recipients, and they must have an email address to enroll successfully. If the record you were trying to enroll is not a person, consider whether it is connected to a person via a relationship attribute. If so, use a variable to select the person via the relationship attribute for the

If the relationship attribute may hold more than one person and you want to enroll all of them, add a Loop block before the Enroll in sequence block and place the Enroll in sequence block inside the Loop.
Learn how to use Loop blocks

A block exceeded the 2-minute maximum execution time. This can affect the Send HTTP request block when an external service is slow to respond. Check whether the external endpoint is available and responding within the time limit. If the service requires more processing time, consider breaking the request into smaller operations. Retry the run if the delay was temporary.

blocks.text: “This workflow does not have permission to write for this object”

segments.t: This appears when a workflow can read from an object but has not been granted write access to update it. Workflows do not automatically inherit write access to every object. To fix this, a workspace member with full access or admin permissions for the relevant object needs to
give the workflow access to the object

lines.t: To update a relationship attribute, the workflow needs write access to the objects on both sides of the relationship.

segments.t: This error appears on the Formula block when one or more variables in the formula have no value. For example, if your formula sums four currency attributes and one is empty, the formula fails because empty is not treated as zero.
To fix this, set a fallback value on each variable in the formula.
In the Formula block, click the variable you want to update.
Repeat for every variable that could be empty when the workflow runs.
Once fallback values are in place, empty attributes are treated as zero and the formula calculates as expected.
This error appears when a block references a variable that had no value at the time the block ran.

One common cause is a workflow with more than one trigger. If a step is connected to both a Record created and a Record updated trigger, but an input on that step only references the output of one of them, the step fails on every run started by the other trigger.
To fix this, add the second trigger's output as another data source on the same variable:

blocks.text: “Please provide a List Entry, not a Record” or similar

segments.t: This error appears when a block receives the wrong type of input. Some blocks expect a list entry and fail if they receive a record. Others expect a specific type of record and fail if they receive a list entry or a different kind of record. For example:
An Update list entry block requires a list entry and will fail if a record is provided.
An Enroll in sequence block requires a person record for the recipient and will fail if a list entry or a different kind of record is provided.
To fix a block that needs a list entry but received a record, add a Find list entries block before the failing block. Configure it with a condition where
and select the record from your previous block as the variable. Then use the output of the Find list entries block as the input for the block that requires a list entry.
You can verify which type a block received by clicking the failed block in the run viewer and checking its

blocks.text: “The provided Record is from a different Object”

segments.t: When a block such as Update record has both an object input and a record input, this error means the record provided belongs to a different object than the one selected. For example, this can happen if the block’s object is set to Companies but receives a person record. Update the object or record so they match.

This error appears on the Send HTTP request block when the request body contains malformed JSON. Common causes include missing or extra commas, unclosed brackets, or incorrect quote characters. To identify the issue, copy the body content and paste it into a JSON validator such as

blocks.text: "Could not update [attribute] as this record is missing the required [attribute] attribute"

segments.t: This error appears when a workflow tries to update a record, but the change is blocked by a rule. The error message identifies the attribute that must have a value for the change to be saved.
Update the workflow to set the required attribute, either in the same block that makes the change or in an earlier block.
Alternatively, use a Filter block to exclude records that don’t meet the rule’s requirements.

faq.q: Why is my workflow run stuck waiting?

segments.t: A run waits when a block needs time, a response, or a decision before the workflow can continue. Open the run in the run viewer to see which block is waiting. The most common reasons are:
Delay and Delay until blocks pause the run for a set duration or until a set date and time. The run continues automatically when the time is reached.
Send request and Slack Send actions blocks pause the run until a recipient selects an action. These blocks show
. Requests don't expire, so the run waits until someone responds or you cancel it.
Agent and AI blocks, such as Custom agent, Web agent, and Classify record, wait while the AI model completes its work. The run continues when the block returns its output.
Blocks from apps can wait for a response from the connected service.
If a run is waiting on something that's no longer needed, you can cancel it. Learn how to
pause, cancel, or resume a run

segments.t: This is your comprehensive guide to understanding and using the building blocks that power
. Workflows gives your team the control and flexibility to build out virtually any go-to-market process you need, right inside Attio.

We’ll break down the various triggers and steps that you can use to automate your processes. At the heart of workflows are two primary components: trigger blocks that initiate the workflow, and steps that execute specific tasks. For a step-by-step walkthrough to set up workflows, see
to understand the feature terms used in these block descriptions.
Workflows are made up of blocks, which define how a workflow runs. Every workflow starts with a trigger block, then continues through one or more steps.

Inputs are the values you configure in the block, such as the object, list, conditions, or instructions. Outputs are the values a block returns during a workflow run, which you can use later in the workflow as variables.
Trigger blocks start a workflow. You can use trigger blocks to start workflows automatically, on a schedule, from an incoming webhook, or manually.
Record triggers start workflows from a specific object, such as Companies, People, or Deals.

Which path is taken in a Switch block?
If multiple paths are true, paths are evaluated in order: Case 1, Case 2, Case 3, then Default. The first path that returns true is the only path that runs.
The Default path is taken if no other case’s conditions are met. If no case conditions are met and there are no blocks on the Default path, the run does not continue past the Switch block.

One use case for this block is assigning work randomly across team members. For example, if you had two Sales team members and want to route half of new leads to each member, you could generate a random number between 0 and 1, follow it with an If block, and when the number is over 0.5 assign to one team member, and when it’s under 0.5 assign to the other team member. Round robin picks one workspace member each time the workflow runs, spreading picks evenly across everyone in the rota.
: Select the workspace members and teams to rotate between. Selecting a team includes everyone in that team. A member who belongs to more than one selected team is counted once.
How the next turn is decided

Round robin picks whoever has gone longest without being picked, so the order you add members and teams in doesn't matter. Anyone who hasn't been picked yet goes first, which means someone newly added to a team is picked next. Teams are resolved on each run, so changing a team changes the rota without editing the workflow. Publishing a new version doesn't restart the rota.

segments.t: Attio only supports direct email syncing with Gmail and Microsoft 365 accounts. It is not possible to connect other email providers or to sync email using standard protocols like SMTP or IMAP.
If you use a different email provider, you can still bring emails into Attio by using our email forwarding feature. Forward emails to your unique inbound Attio address to:

faq.q: Is anything lost if I remove a synced account, then sync it again?

segments.t: Yes, a few things will be lost if you remove a synced account and then sync it again:
Calendar events that were connected to notes will be removed and will not be reconnected automatically.
Emails that were manually shared before removing the account will no longer be shared.
Emails or calendar events that were deleted from the mailbox or calendar will not show in Attio after re-syncing.

faq.q: What happens if a former teammate’s email address is added as an alias for another user?

segments.t: Adding a former teammate’s email address as an alias to an active user does not restore or transfer historical emails. Any emails that were previously synced from the former teammate’s mailbox are removed when their account is suspended or removed.

Going forward, if new emails sent to that address arrive in the active user’s connected mailbox, those emails will appear in Attio. They will be attributed to the active user whose mailbox is synced, not to the removed teammate.
Aliases only affect how new emails are detected and attributed. They do not cause Attio to resync or recover past emails.

faq.q: Can I choose to only sync certain emails?

segments.t: , Attio will only create records and sync in emails when you've sent an email to someone or had a calendar event with them. If someone has only emailed you and you’ve never replied, no record is created.

It can help to think of People and Companies as a representation of your broader network rather than something you manage record by record. With email sync enabled, Attio captures context automatically so nothing is missed and conversations are available whenever you need them.
Day to day work typically happens in deals, lists,

The result is less manual upkeep, better context across your workspace, and a system that stays focused on the records that matter.

faq.q: Can I use Attio as a shared inbox or sync a shared email address like team@?

segments.t: Attio works best for giving your team a shared view of relationships and communication history, rather than managing a collaborative team mailbox.

Shared inbox platforms are designed to help multiple teammates manage a single email address with features like assignment, internal notes, and workflow rules. In Attio, each user connects their own mailbox and can choose to share email visibility with teammates, but sending and receiving always happens through an individual’s connected mailbox.

You can sync a shared email address only if it has its own login credentials. For example, a Gmail-based shared mailbox with its own username and password can be connected by one Attio user. Only that user will be able to send from it, and communication insights such as last interaction and connection strength will be tied to their account. Microsoft 365 shared mailboxes cannot be synced directly because they do not have separate login credentials.

faq.q: Why does an email appear to be stuck in the outbox?

segments.t: If an email in your outbox appears to be stuck and you have not reached Attio’s hourly, daily, or plan-based
, the cause may be a rate limit enforced by your email provider.
Email providers such as Gmail apply their own sending limits at the mailbox level. These limits are separate from Attio’s limits and are shared across all apps connected to that mailbox via OAuth.

If another connected app sends a high volume of email and reaches the provider’s rate limit, the provider may temporarily reject additional send requests. This can prevent Attio from sending emails until the provider’s limit resets.
If you suspect this is happening, review other tools connected to the same mailbox and wait for the provider’s rate limit window to reset. Attio will send the email once the rate limit has cleared.

faq.q: Can I resend an email from the Failed page?

It failed before August 12, 2026. Attio started recording failure reasons on that date.
You have more than 300 failures. The
page shows only your 300 most recent.
It was sent as part of a sequence. Sequence emails appear in the sequence itself, not on the
It was sent from a mailbox you haven't synced. You only see emails sent from your own synced mailboxes.

faq.q: Why aren’t my emails showing up? Some emails seem to be missing in Attio.

segments.t: If you're not seeing certain emails in Attio, follow these steps to troubleshoot:
1. Check if your email sync is active
and confirm your mailbox shows "In sync".
If it shows as disconnected or says Attio does not have adequate permissions,
follow these steps to reconnect your mailbox
2. Email sync is active, and the email is missing from a person record
Does the email include an address that matches one listed on the person’s record? With default settings, emails will only appear if there's a matching email address on the record.
Has anyone in the email thread been blocklisted? If any participant’s email address or domain is blocklisted, it can hide the email.
3. Email sync is active, and the email is missing from a company record

With default settings, emails will only appear on a company record if at least one participant has an email domain that matches the company's domain. Even if you've manually linked a person to the company, their emails will not show unless their domain matches. To ensure all team members' emails show on companies regardless of their email domains, admins can add Team > Email addresses as an additional source for the Emails tab on companies by
Blocklisting also applies here. If a participant is blocklisted, the email may not appear.
4. If you are using email forwarding instead of sync

Emails forwarded to Attio will only appear on the records of participants included in the most recent message of the forwarded thread. If someone forwards you a message and you then forward that into Attio, it will be added to the record of the person who forwarded it to you, not the original sender.
You must forward emails from the same email address you use to log into Attio. Emails forwarded from other addresses will not appear.
If you're still having trouble, contact us at
and we’ll be happy to assist.

faq.q: Do I need to keep someone's old email address on their record in order for those emails to remain in Attio?

segments.t: Yes. Attio only displays emails that match the addresses listed in the record's email addresses attribute. If you remove an email address from a record, any emails associated with that address will also be removed from view.

If the event is not private and is missing from a company record, check the participant list. At least one invited email address must use a domain that matches the domain stored on the company’s record.
